vignette: The retaining wall groans first. Mateo is twenty-four, of Mexican-American descent, when the parking structure behind the neighborhood infrastructure fair gives way. One moment, the air smells of diesel and roasted corn; the next, a sound like tearing metal screams through the lot. Concrete pours down like a slow tide. He remembers the weight first-a support column crushing his left shoulder, the sudden, suffocating dark, the taste of chalk and copper. He remembers counting his breaths through a crack in the slab, listening to the distant wail of sirens muffle into silence, waiting for hands that never came fast enough. His cousin, who helped him load the crates, does not pull him out. He wakes in a hospital three days later. When Mateo returns to his apartment, he stops answering calls from anyone who works in construction or property management. He moves his phone to airplane mode for hours at a time, terrified that a ringtone will trigger the same suffocating dread. At night, he sleeps in his closet, stacked boxes forming a barrier, a heavy flashlight within arm's reach. He tells himself it is practical, but his body knows better; his pulse races at the sound of settling pipes, his jaw clenches at the hum of elevators, his breath shortens when the wind shifts outside his window. He tells his abuela he is fine, but he stops attending family gatherings near the city center, finding the crowded streets feel like a pressure chamber waiting to rupture. He lands a job as a QA Engineer six months later, which initially feels like a safe harbor. The work demands precision: he spends his days writing test scripts, stress-testing software for structural integrity, and documenting every flaw before deployment. But the overlap between his profession and his nervous system is relentless. When a system crashes during his testing, he does not just see a bug. He feels the floor drop, hears the concrete crack, and spends twenty minutes staring at the blank monitor while his hands shake. He has begun double-checking his own code forty times, convinced that if he misses one variable, the entire architecture will fail just like that wall. His colleagues notice he never takes lunch in the break room, preferring to work at his desk with noise-canceling headphones on, watching grainy footage of empty commercial lots on a secondary monitor to "keep his edge." In session, Mateo describes the present as a series of close calls that never happen. He avoids crosswalks near tall buildings, routes his morning commute through familiar, low-rise neighborhoods, and checks the seismic history of every restaurant before agreeing to dinner. He tells me about a recent date that ended early when her apartment building undergoes fire inspection drills, noting how his chest tightened until he could no longer pretend to listen. He does not blame her. He simply says he needs to be somewhere he can breathe. He has been single since the incident, not out of disinterest, but because intimacy requires leaning forward, and he has spent years bracing for collapse. Now, he sits in the chair, shoulders slowly dropping as he watches me take notes. The room is quiet. He asks if the foundation of this building was reinforced, then immediately covers his mouth, laughing softly at himself. He does not look away. His breathing slows. The tapping of his fingers stops. He stays.
